front: How do esophageal squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma differ in location and main risk factors?
back: SCC: upper/mid esophagus, from smoking and alcohol. Adenocarcinoma: distal esophagus/GEJ, from GERD, Barrett's, and obesity.
extra: SCC dominates worldwide; adenocarcinoma dominates in the US. SCC is more radiosensitive.

front: What causes most anal cancers, and who is at highest risk?
back: HPV (mostly HPV-16); people with HIV are at highest risk.
extra: Also other immunosuppression, smoking, and prior cervical, vulvar, or vaginal dysplasia or cancer. Symptoms are often blamed on hemorrhoids.

front: Anal and rectal cancer are neighbors. How do they differ in histology and in the curative treatment?
back: Anal cancer is HPV-driven squamous cell carcinoma cured with definitive chemoradiation. Rectal cancer is adenocarcinoma, where surgery is the central curative step.
extra: For anal cancer, surgery is salvage. For rectal cancer, chemoRT prepares for surgery (or organ preservation).

front: What is the classic presentation of a pancreatic head cancer?
back: Painless jaundice
extra: Body/tail tumors present later with back pain and weight loss. New-onset diabetes with weight loss after 50 is a red flag. Smoking is the biggest modifiable risk factor.

front: What is the usual background for hepatocellular carcinoma?
back: Cirrhosis (from hepatitis B or C, alcohol, or fatty liver)
extra: Hepatitis B can cause HCC without cirrhosis. Liver function often limits treatment as much as the tumor does.

front: Why do esophageal radiation fields use long margins up and down but short margins sideways?
back: A longitudinal submucosal lymphatic network lets tumor spread several cm along the esophagus.
extra: Typical CTV: about 3-4 cm up and down, ~1 cm radially. The esophagus also lacks a serosa, so it reaches the mediastinum early.

front: Why does a low rectal tumor (within about 5 cm of the anal verge) matter for treatment?
back: It may need an abdominoperineal resection with a permanent colostomy, so it is a prime candidate for organ-preserving neoadjuvant therapy.
extra: Height is measured from the anal verge: low 0-5 cm, mid 5-10 cm, upper 10-15 cm. Upper rectal tumors above the peritoneal reflection behave more like colon cancer.

front: What is the mesorectal fascia, and why does it matter?
back: The envelope around the mesorectum. It is the plane of total mesorectal excision (TME), so it acts as the surgical margin.
extra: Tumor close to it on MRI is a threatened margin, the strongest predictor of local recurrence.

front: What landmark splits the lymphatic drainage of the anal canal?
back: The dentate line: above it drains to mesorectal/internal iliac nodes, below it to the inguinal nodes.

front: Are inguinal nodes regional for anal cancer? For rectal cancer?
back: Anal: yes, always regional and always in the field. Rectal: no, they are distant (M1) unless the tumor invades the anal canal.
extra: External iliac nodes follow the same rule: regional for anal, nonregional for rectal.

front: What does the standard rectal cancer radiation target include?
back: The tumor, the entire mesorectum, and the presacral, internal iliac, and obturator nodes
extra: Add external iliac nodes for T4 tumors invading anterior organs, and inguinal nodes if the anal canal is involved.

front: What is the key local staging study for rectal cancer, and what does it report?
back: High-resolution pelvic MRI: T stage, distance to the mesorectal fascia, EMVI, involved nodes, and height from the anal verge
extra: A restaging MRI with endoscopy after neoadjuvant therapy decides who can try watch-and-wait.

front: On rectal MRI, when is the mesorectal fascia (circumferential margin) "threatened"?
back: When tumor, a node, a tumor deposit, or EMVI is within 1 mm of it
extra: A threatened margin pushes toward total neoadjuvant therapy, usually with long-course chemoRT.

front: What is EMVI in rectal cancer, and what does it predict?
back: Extramural venous invasion: tumor in veins outside the rectal wall. It predicts distant metastases.
extra: EMVI and tumor deposits predict distant recurrence better than nodal status.

front: What is the best test for the depth of an esophageal cancer, and why does T1a matter?
back: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). T1a (mucosa only) can be removed endoscopically; T1b and deeper need surgery or chemoRT.
extra: PET/CT adds nodal and distant staging and helps define tumor length for contouring.

front: What does a pancreatic-protocol CT show that decides the treatment plan?
back: How much the tumor touches the major arteries and veins, which decides resectability
extra: Thin-slice arterial and portal venous phases. Get it before a biliary stent if possible, because stent inflammation blurs the edges.

front: When can hepatocellular carcinoma be diagnosed without a biopsy?
back: In a cirrhotic liver, when multiphase CT or MRI shows arterial hyperenhancement with washout (LI-RADS 5)
extra: HCC enhances early because it is fed by the hepatic artery.

front: What pattern does TNM staging follow for most GI cancers?
back: T = depth through the wall layers; N = number of involved regional nodes; M = distant spread
extra: Wall layers: mucosa → submucosa → muscularis propria → beyond the wall → adjacent organs.

front: How does anal cancer staging break the usual GI pattern?
back: T is by tumor size (≤2, >2-5, >5 cm, T4 = invades adjacent organs), and N is by node location, not number.
extra: Treatment is chemoRT for nearly every stage, so the stage mainly shapes the dose.

front: How is pancreatic cancer "staged" in practice?
back: By resectability: no arterial contact and limited vein contact = resectable; >180° contact with the SMA or celiac axis (or an unreconstructable vein) = locally advanced; in between = borderline.
extra: Decided by multidisciplinary review of the pancreatic-protocol CT. Any distant metastasis makes it unresectable.

front: Which staging system is used for hepatocellular carcinoma, and what does it combine?
back: BCLC: tumor burden, liver function (Child-Pugh), and performance status
extra: Each BCLC stage maps to a treatment. TNM does not drive pretreatment decisions in HCC.

front: Why is diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal washings done before curative gastric cancer surgery?
back: CT misses peritoneal disease, and positive peritoneal cytology alone makes it M1 (stage IV).

front: Which biomarker changes rectal cancer management the most, and how?
back: MMR deficiency (MSI-high): these patients get immunotherapy first.
extra: With dostarlimab alone, essentially all patients in the Cercek study had a complete clinical response. MMR deficiency can be hereditary (Lynch syndrome), which also causes endometrial, ovarian, gastric, and urinary tract cancers.

front: Which tumor markers are followed in pancreatic, colorectal, and liver cancer?
back: Pancreas: CA 19-9. Colorectal: CEA. HCC: AFP.
extra: CA 19-9 is unreliable with jaundice and absent in Lewis-antigen-negative patients.

front: What is the standard treatment for anal squamous cell carcinoma?
back: Definitive chemoradiation with 5-FU (or capecitabine) and mitomycin, including the groins and pelvic nodes
extra: Nigro showed chemoRT could replace abdominoperineal resection; APR is saved for persistent or recurrent disease.

front: How long after anal cancer chemoradiation should you wait before calling residual disease?
back: Up to about 26 weeks, because tumors keep shrinking for months
extra: ACT II. Persistent or progressing disease gets a biopsy and salvage APR.

front: What is the most prominent acute side effect of anal cancer chemoradiation?
back: A severe perineal and groin skin reaction
extra: Also diarrhea and low blood counts (mitomycin). Avoid treatment breaks, which lower cure rates.

front: Does early (T1-T2 N0) rectal cancer need radiation?
back: Not routinely: it goes straight to TME surgery.
extra: Exception: a low tumor where the patient wants to avoid a stoma may get neoadjuvant therapy aiming for organ preservation.

front: What are the short-course and long-course radiation options for rectal cancer?
back: Short-course: 25 Gy in 5 fractions without chemo. Long-course: 45-50.4 Gy in 25-28 fractions with capecitabine.
extra: Long-course is preferred for a threatened margin or T4 tumor.

front: Which organ at risk most limits pelvic radiation for rectal cancer, and how is it moved out of the field?
back: The small bowel; treating with a full bladder (and sometimes prone) pushes bowel up and out of the pelvis.
extra: Other OARs: bladder and femoral heads. Small bowel dose drives diarrhea and late bowel injury.

front: For locally advanced rectal cancer, is chemoradiation better before or after surgery?
back: Before: preoperative chemoRT gave better local control with less toxicity, and the same survival.
extra: German CAO/ARO/AIO-94.

front: What is total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) for rectal cancer?
back: Giving all the chemotherapy and radiation before surgery
extra: RAPIDO (fewer treatment failures) and PRODIGE 23 (better survival). It is followed by TME, or watch-and-wait after a complete response. MRI features that push toward TNT: T4, a threatened mesorectal fascia, EMVI, N2 or lateral pelvic nodes, or a low tumor where organ preservation is the goal.

front: What is "watch-and-wait" in rectal cancer?
back: Skipping TME surgery after a complete clinical response to neoadjuvant therapy, with close endoscopy and MRI surveillance and surgery if the tumor regrows
extra: In OPRA, about half of patients kept their rectum; chemoRT followed by consolidation chemo did best.

front: What is the CROSS regimen for esophageal cancer?
back: Neoadjuvant chemoradiation (41.4 Gy in 23 fractions with weekly carboplatin/paclitaxel), then esophagectomy
extra: Nearly doubled median survival. SCC responds best. For adenocarcinoma, perioperative FLOT is an alternative (ESOPEC).

front: Who gets definitive (non-surgical) chemoradiation for esophageal cancer, and to what dose?
back: Cervical esophageal tumors, squamous cell cancers, T4b tumors, and patients unfit for surgery; about 50-50.4 Gy
extra: RTOG 8501: chemoRT beat RT alone. RTOG 9405: 64.8 Gy was no better than 50.4 Gy.

front: What is the role of radiation in gastric cancer?
back: Limited: adjuvant chemoRT after an inadequate node dissection or a positive margin, and palliation of bleeding
extra: The standard is perioperative FLOT chemotherapy with D2 gastrectomy; adding postoperative chemoRT after that didn't help (CRITICS). Typical palliative courses for bleeding: 8 Gy × 1-2 up to 30 Gy in 10.

front: In locally advanced pancreatic cancer, what does radiation (chemoRT or SBRT) after chemo accomplish?
back: Better local control and pain relief, but no proven survival benefit
extra: LAP07. Pancreatic cancer treatment is chemo-led. The duodenum and bowel next to the pancreas limit SBRT dose.

front: When is SBRT used for hepatocellular carcinoma, and what patient factor limits it?
back: For tumors not suited to resection or ablation, as a bridge to transplant, or for portal vein thrombus; limited by liver function (Child-Pugh A to B7)
extra: RTOG 1112: SBRT + sorafenib improved survival. Enough normal liver must be spared to avoid radiation-induced liver disease.
